questions: Does max_error still cluster at about 0.06 m on every track? If so, the limit is turn authority rather than sensing.
Did the narrower track increase steering_oscillation (jitter) without line loss? If so, the controller needs less kp or more kd.
Did the robot reach tight bends at lower speed, or did it reach them at full speed and then leave the line?
Did line_loss_events stay near 1 on the s-bend with the five-sensor row? If so, the sensor row is still too narrow at the bends.

intent: Revert to the iteration 0 five-sensor row (best score, 136) and test turn authority with a narrower wheel_track (0.10 m) and lighter mass (0.6 kg). Narrower track raises yaw rate per unit wheel-speed difference, and lower mass lowers yaw inertia. Expected result: max_error below 0.06 m on oval and s-bend, more completions, and higher progress than iteration 1. Gains and base_speed remain the Integrator's choice.
learning: Iteration 0 to 1 showed that a wider sensor row reduces line loss but does not stop off-track exits, because the 0.06 m limit is fixed by the body geometry. Test whether yaw response (wheel_track and mass) is the binding limit. If narrowing the track and lowering mass raises completions, turn authority is the lever. If max_error stays at 0.06 m with no change, look at base_speed (set by the Integrator) rather than geometry.
rationale: Evidence from iterations 0 and 1: widening the sensor row to ±0.06 m (iteration 1) cut line-loss events (oval 1.0 to 0.4, s-bend 1.1 to 0.2, slalom 1.0 to 0.55), but every trial still ended off track. Progress fell (oval 0.64 to 0.38, s-bend 0.21 to 0.14), the only completion was lost (1 of 60 trials across both iterations), and the score dropped from 136 to 86. Sensing was therefore not the binding limit. Max_error sits at 0.0615 to 0.0635 m in every trial of both designs. The off-track limit is max(0.06, 0.0125 + body_width/4). Even at the maximum body_width of 0.18 m that gives 0.0575, so the limit stays at 0.06 m. The robot is being lost at the same lateral error whatever the sensors report, which points to turn authority or yaw response. The contract gives turn rate = (v_R - v_L)/wheel_track, so for the same PWM difference a narrower track yaws faster. Yaw inertia scales with mass*(L²+W²)/12, so a lighter body also turns more readily. My R1 feedback suggested widening wheel_track to 0.14 m for more turn authority. The contract physics point the other way, so I am not following that suggestion. I will revert the sensor row to the better-scoring five-sensor ±0.04 m layout and make one change to the turning dynamics: narrow wheel_track from 0.12 to 0.10 m and reduce mass from 0.8 to 0.6 kg. I expect more yaw per unit of turn command, so the robot should track tighter bends and hold max_error below 0.06 m, giving more completions and higher progress.
